opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the things that surprised me most, honestly. When we started LeRobot, I assumed the community would mostly be roboticists, people with a mechanical engineering or controls background who'd been building robots for years. And some of them came, of course. But a really big chunk of the people who showed up were coming from the AI side. They'd been fine-tuning language models, playing with diffusion models, hanging out on the Hub, and suddenly they realized: wait, I can buy a cheap arm, plug it in, record some demonstrations, and train a policy with the same kind of tools I already know.

What I find interesting about that is they don't carry the same assumptions. Traditional robotics has a very strong culture around modeling the system precisely: kinematics, dynamics, carefully engineered control loops. That's all valuable, but it also means you sometimes think a problem is too hard before you've tried it. The people coming from AI just think, "Well, let's collect data and train an end-to-end model and see what happens." Sometimes that's naive, but quite often it works better than you'd expect, and that's how you find out where the field actually is.

And they bring the open-source habits with them. They share their datasets, they upload their checkpoints, they post videos of their failures. That's something robotics has historically been weak at, partly because hardware is expensive and every lab has its own setup, so nothing is reproducible. If you have thousands of people with similar low-cost arms, all sharing data in the same format, you start building the kind of collective dataset that robotics has never really had. That's very much what happened with NLP: the breakthroughs came once there was a shared ecosystem of data and models. So these newcomers aren't just users. In a way they're the ones who might make robotics feel more like AI did ten years ago: messy, fast, very open, with a lot of people trying things at the same time.

fable-5.1.text:
What I find fascinating is that these people are coming at robotics from the complete opposite direction than the field traditionally expects. For decades, robotics was a hardware-first discipline. You learned control theory, you learned kinematics, you spent years with a specific arm or a specific platform, and the "intelligence" layer was something you bolted on at the end, often as a bunch of hand-tuned heuristics.

The folks arriving through LeRobot mostly don't have that background. They come from language models, from diffusion models, from training transformers on large datasets. Their instinct is: show me the data, show me the model, let me fine-tune it, let me iterate. And they bring that mindset to a physical system. So they'll pick up a cheap arm, collect a few hundred demonstrations with a leader-follower setup, train a policy over a weekend, and share it on the Hub. That workflow is completely natural to them because it's exactly how they've been doing NLP or vision for years.

And I think that's really healthy for the field, for two reasons. First, they don't carry the baggage of what's "supposed" to be hard. A lot of them don't know that something was considered impossible five years ago, so they just try it, and sometimes it works. Second, they're used to open ecosystems. In AI, the norm became sharing weights, sharing datasets, writing reproducible training code. Robotics historically was much more closed, with each lab having its own setup and results that nobody could reproduce. These newcomers expect the open model by default, and they're kind of forcing the field to adopt it.

The flip side, and this is also what makes it interesting, is that they hit the wall of the physical world very quickly. Data is expensive, you can't just scrape it. A policy that looks great in evaluation fails because the lighting changed or the gripper has slightly different friction. So they go through this education where they discover that the real world doesn't behave like a dataset. And watching that collision, between the AI mindset and the messiness of hardware, is where I think a lot of the real progress is going to come from. It's a bit like when the deep learning people came into NLP and didn't respect the linguists' rules at first, then gradually we all learned from each other. I think we're at that moment in robotics now.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re interesting because they come in with a different set of assumptions. If you come from AI, your instinct is to ask: can we learn this from data? Can we share datasets and models, and improve them together? And robotics gives you a very concrete way to test those ideas. You can have a model that looks impressive on a screen, but getting a robot to pick something up reliably is a different challenge.

With LeRobot, we want to make it easier for those people to start experimenting without first having to become experts in every part of robotics. And I’m curious about what happens when they meet people who have that robotics experience. One group brings new ideas about learning, the other understands the physical constraints. That exchange can be really productive.

sol-6.1.text: What I find interesting is that they come with a different set of assumptions. If you come from AI, you tend to ask, “Can we learn this from data?” You might not know all the reasons a roboticist would tell you something is difficult, so you try things that people with more experience might not try. Of course, you then discover that the physical world is quite unforgiving. But that meeting between people who understand the hardware and people who bring this learning-first approach is very exciting. With LeRobot, we want to make it easier for those communities to work together—to share datasets, share models, and build on each other’s experiments.
